title: Counting the Complement
short: Count "at least one" as all the possibilities minus the ones with none.
trouble: Students count committees with at least one woman by choosing one woman first and then anyone at all, which counts the same committee several times.

blocks.html: "At least one" problems are everywhere: committees with at least one woman, passwords with at least one digit. Counting them head-on means many cases. Counting the opposite is usually one short step, built from the sum rule and combinations.
To count the outcomes with a property, count all outcomes and subtract those without it: $$\#(\text{at least one}) = \#(\text{all}) - \#(\text{none}).$$

Listen for the words "at least one," "some," "not all" and "contains a." Each is the opposite of a simple condition (none, all, never), and that opposite is usually a single product. A password with no digit is just a string of letters; a committee with no women is just a committee of men; a sequence of dice rolls with no 6 has $5$ choices per roll.

Every outcome either has at least one of the thing or has none, never both. So by the sum rule, all $=$ (none) $+$ (at least one). Rearranging gives the formula. The "none" case is usually simple: a committee with no women is just a committee chosen from the men.

blocks.name: disc-overcount
blocks.cap: A tempting shortcut that overcounts: "choose one woman first, then anyone." A committee with two women is produced twice, once for each woman picked first.

blocks.title: Committees with at least one woman
blocks.q: A committee of $3$ is chosen from $4$ women and $3$ men. How many committees include at least one woman?
steps: No women: all three from the $3$ men, $\binom{3}{3} = 1$.

blocks.title: Bit strings
blocks.q: How many bit strings of length $8$ contain at least one 1? At least two 1s?
steps: All strings: $2^{8} = 256$. The only string with no 1 is 00000000, so at least one 1: $255$.
"At least two 1s" is the opposite of "zero or one 1." There is $1$ string with no 1 and $8$ with exactly one (choose its position).

blocks.title: Repeated digits
blocks.q: How many $4$-digit PINs (digits 0–9) have at least one repeated digit?

blocks.html: Choosing "one first, then anyone." For the committees above it is tempting to pick a woman ($4$ ways) and then any $2$ of the other $6$ people ($\binom{6}{2} = 15$), giving $60$. But the committee $\{W_{1}, W_{2}, M_{1}\}$ is produced twice: once with $W_{1}$ picked first and once with $W_{2}$. Committees with more women are counted more times, so $60$ is far too big. Check: a correct method produces each outcome exactly once; ask how many ways your method can produce one particular outcome.
